overview: Airbus SE is a Dutch-incorporated, European aerospace and defense group headquartered operationally in Toulouse, France (registered seat Leiden, Netherlands), listed on Euronext Paris, Deutsche Borse (Xetra) and the Spanish exchanges. It designs, manufactures and sells commercial aircraft (A220, A320 family, A330, A350), civil and military helicopters, and defense/space systems (military aircraft, satellites, space systems, cyber/intelligence). Commercial Aircraft is by far the dominant segment (roughly 72% of FY2025 revenue of EUR73.4bn), with Defence and Space (~18%) and Helicopters (~12%) rounding out the group; the commercial order backlog stood at a record 8,754 aircraft at year-end 2025 (9,222 by mid-2026), providing many years of revenue visibility.

business_model.summary: Airbus manufactures and sells large commercial jetliners, helicopters, and military/space systems, monetizing a huge multi-year order backlog through aircraft deliveries, plus recurring aftermarket services, spares, maintenance, upgrades and financing support. Revenue is predominantly project/delivery-based (aircraft are built against firm orders and revenue is recognized largely on delivery), but a growing services/support tail (spares, MRO, training, digital) provides a more recurring, higher-margin layer across all three segments.

revenue_streams.name: Defence and Space (military aircraft, space systems, cyber/intelligence)

business_model.customer_type: B2B — airlines (full-service and low-cost carriers), leasing companies, governments and defense ministries, and institutional/space customers
business_model.geographic_mix: Global commercial aircraft customer base (Asia-Pacific, Europe, Americas, Middle East); manufacturing concentrated in France, Germany, Spain, UK and the US (Mobile, Alabama) and China (Tianjin FAL); Defence and Space customers concentrated in Europe (France, Germany, Spain, UK) and NATO allies

main_competitors: Lockheed Martin / Leonardo / Thales / RTX-Collins (Defence and Space)
competitive_position.market_position: Effective duopoly with Boeing in large commercial jet aircraft; global leader (and near-monopoly in practice) in the single-aisle/narrowbody segment while Boeing works through 737 MAX and 787 production and quality problems; #1 or #2 in civil/military helicopters; mid-tier player relative to US primes in defense and a developing/loss-recovering position in space systems.

moat_factors.description: Designing, certifying and mass-producing a commercial jetliner requires decades of expertise, enormous capital and regulatory approval (EASA/FAA/CAAC); only Airbus and Boeing currently do this at scale globally

Record backlog of ~8,750-9,200+ aircraft (roughly 8-9 years of production at current rates) locks in revenue; airlines standardize fleets around a single-aisle platform (common type ratings, spares, training, MRO infrastructure) making switching between Airbus/Boeing costly

moat_factors.factor: Narrowbody leadership while Boeing is distracted
moat_factors.description: Boeing's 737 MAX safety/quality issues and FAA production cap, plus 787 production problems, have let Airbus take outsized share of narrowbody orders and deliveries in recent years

In-house engineering, final assembly lines on three continents, and (post-Spirit acquisition) greater control over structures/fuselage work packages reduce single-supplier dependency, though engine supply remains externalized to CFM/Pratt & Whitney/Rolls-Royce
French, German and Spanish state shareholdings and golden-share-like protections provide political and financing support, especially relevant for Defence and Space

weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a small number of engine suppliers (CFM, Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce, Safran) whose capacity shortfalls directly cap Airbus's own production and delivery rates
Defence and Space has structurally lower margins than Commercial Aircraft and has suffered recurring charges/impairments (OneSat satellites, A400M legacy losses)
Newly internalized Spirit AeroSystems structures business brings integration, cost-absorption and labor-relations risk
Geopolitically exposed supply chain and large USD-denominated cost/revenue mismatches given EUR functional currency
Long-term, distant but real risk from Chinese state-backed COMAC C919 in the narrowbody segment, especially in China's huge domestic market

growth_drivers: A320 Family production rate ramp toward 70-75 aircraft/month by end-2027 (stabilizing at 75), the single largest driver of delivery and revenue growth
A220 ramp toward 13/month by 2028, A330 toward rate 5 by 2029, and A350 toward rate 12 by 2028
Record commercial order backlog (9,222 aircraft at H1 2026) providing multi-year revenue visibility and pricing power
Widebody (A350/A330neo) demand recovery as long-haul travel and international capacity continue to normalize/grow

European and allied defense spending increases (NATO commitments, European rearmament) driving record Defence and Space order intake (EUR17.7bn in FY2025, EUR9.3bn in H1 2026 alone) and improving segment margins
Growing aftermarket/services revenue (spares, upgrades, digital, training, fleet support) across all segments, which is higher-margin and more recurring than new-build deliveries
Full ownership of former Spirit AeroSystems structures work packages (A350, A220, A321, A320 wing components) improving supply security and long-term cost control
Potential further consolidation in European space (MoU with Leonardo and Thales for satellite business) to rationalize costs and improve space segment profitability
Helicopters segment military order momentum supplementing civil rotorcraft demand

business.risk: Engine supplier constraints (Pratt & Whitney GTF, CFM LEAP)
business.description: Pratt & Whitney shortages (partly due to prioritizing MRO over new engines) and historical CFM/Safran disruptions are the binding constraint on A320 Family output, repeatedly pushing back rate targets
Simultaneously ramping A220, A320 family, A330 and A350 rates requires flawless supply chain, labor and facility execution; delays have repeatedly occurred across the industry post-COVID

December 2025 acquisition of Spirit's Airbus-related structures business brings integration costs, a EUR749m FY2025 charge (A220 intangible impairment plus onerous-contract provisions) tied to the shift from 'buy' to 'make' cost accounting, and ongoing purchase price allocation finalization through end-2026

History of cost overruns and impairments (OneSat satellite program, A400M legacy losses ~EUR477m in a prior year) though A400M is now said to be approaching sustainable profitability; ~2,500 planned job cuts in the division carry execution/labor risk
C919 remains uncertified outside China and produced at low rates, but represents a multi-decade risk to Airbus/Boeing narrowbody duopoly, particularly in the large protected Chinese domestic market
Revenue concentrated among global airlines and lessors; a sharp downturn in air travel demand or airline financial distress could trigger order deferrals or cancellations

financial.risk: FX exposure (EUR costs vs USD aircraft pricing)
financial.description: Airbus reports in EUR but commercial aircraft are priced and largely sold in USD; the company uses extensive hedging (large cash flow hedge reserves swung EUR5.4bn favorably in FY2025 other comprehensive income) but earnings remain sensitive to EUR/USD moves and hedge roll-off
Material defined benefit pension obligations subject to discount-rate and asset-return volatility, flowing through other comprehensive income

financial.risk: Working capital swings tied to production ramp
financial.description: H1 2026 free cash flow before customer financing was negative (-EUR1,166m) largely due to inventory build for the ramp-up; free cash flow is seasonally and cyclically volatile around delivery timing

regulatory.description: US-origin content (engines, avionics) subjects some Airbus aircraft to US export control (ITAR/EAR) rules, constraining sales to certain sanctioned countries; defense exports also face case-by-case government approval
FY2026 guidance explicitly incorporates 'currently applicable tariffs,' implying real but currently quantified cost/pricing impact from US/EU trade measures on aerospace goods
EASA/FAA certification requirements are a barrier to new entrants (a moat) but also create risk of program delays if new aircraft or derivative certifications are held up

macro.description: Commercial aircraft demand is tied to global GDP growth, fuel prices, and air travel demand; a severe downturn (as in 2020) sharply reduces deliveries, cancels orders and triggers deferrals

Airbus provides limited direct customer/sales financing exposure (hence guidance is stated 'before customer financing' impacts) and carries net cash, limiting direct rate sensitivity, though higher rates can pressure airline customers' aircraft financing costs
Exposure to titanium, aluminum, composite materials and energy costs; geopolitical disruption (e.g., Russia-linked titanium supply historically) can affect input availability and cost

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Commercial aerospace remains in a multi-year up-cycle: global air traffic continues to grow, both Airbus and Boeing have order backlogs stretching 8+ years, and neither OEM can currently meet demand due to supply chain constraints rather than lack of orders. Defense spending is rising across Europe and NATO allies, providing a secular tailwind to the smaller Defence and Space and Helicopters segments.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high over a full cycle (commercial aviation is capital-goods/cyclical and was severely impacted by COVID-19), but currently cushioned by a record backlog that provides multi-year revenue visibility largely independent of near-term demand swings; defense revenue is comparatively non-cyclical/counter-cyclical
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate direct sensitivity given net cash position and limited balance-sheet customer financing exposure; indirect sensitivity via airline customers' financing costs and aircraft leasing economics

recent_developments.event: Completed acquisition of certain Spirit AeroSystems businesses tied to Airbus supply contracts (Kinston NC, St. Nazaire, Casablanca, Wichita, Belfast, Prestwick sites), recognizing a US$856m non-cash gain on extinguishment of the prior supply agreement alongside a EUR749m Q4 2025 charge (EUR500m A220 intangible impairment plus EUR249m onerous-contract provisions) from the 'buy-to-make' cost reassessment

Reported FY2025 results: revenue EUR73.4bn (+6% YoY), EBIT Adjusted EUR7.1bn, net income EUR5.22bn (attributable), 793 commercial aircraft delivered, record order backlog of 8,754 aircraft, gross orders of 1,000 (889 net), consolidated order intake value of EUR123.3bn; met FY2025 guidance; proposed dividend of EUR3.20/share

Issued FY2026 guidance (before M&A, including then-applicable tariffs): ~870 commercial aircraft deliveries, EBIT Adjusted ~EUR7.5bn, free cash flow before customer financing ~EUR4.5bn; flagged Pratt & Whitney GTF engine shortages as the primary constraint on A320 Family ramp, pushing the 70-75/month target out to end-2027

Announced memorandum of understanding with Leonardo and Thales (October 2025/continuing into 2026) to explore consolidation of European satellite manufacturing operations, aimed at addressing chronic Space Systems losses (OneSat program charges)

H1 2026 results: revenue EUR33.2bn (+12% YoY), EBIT Adjusted EUR2,727m, net income EUR2,243m (EPS EUR2.84), 351 commercial aircraft delivered (vs 306 H1 2025), backlog grew to 9,222 aircraft; Defence and Space EBIT Adjusted nearly doubled to EUR487m on record order intake; free cash flow before customer financing remained negative (-EUR1,166m) on ramp-related inventory build; FY2026 guidance reaffirmed

Airbus outpaced Boeing on both deliveries and new orders through much of 2026 as Boeing continued working through 737 MAX and 787 production/quality recovery, though Boeing's 737 MAX monthly rate has been climbing toward the FAA-approved cap of 42/month

guidance.as_of: H1 2026 results (reaffirmed FY2025 guidance issued February 2026)

items.notes: Reaffirmed at H1 2026 (351 delivered in H1); constrained primarily by Pratt & Whitney GTF engine shortages; FY2025 actual was 793
Up from FY2025 actual of EUR7.1bn; guidance stated before M&A and includes currently applicable tariffs

items.metric: Free Cash Flow before Customer Financing
items.notes: H1 2026 FCF before customer financing was -EUR1,166m, reflecting normal seasonal/ramp-related inventory build; full-year target assumes H2-weighted delivery and cash generation as is typical
Delayed due to Pratt & Whitney GTF engine supply shortages; Airbus has said it is pursuing contractual remedies with Pratt & Whitney
Also previously trimmed from higher ambitions; now supported by in-housed Belfast/Wichita work packages post-Spirit acquisition
Widebody ramp supported by in-housed Kinston/St. Nazaire fuselage sections post-Spirit acquisition
Slower widebody program relative to A350
Proposed to AGM on 14 April 2026; reflects FY2025 net income growth

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Guillaume Faury described Airbus as 'ramping up across all businesses to meet the growing demand for our civil and military solutions' and credited 'steady execution' for strong Q2 2026 deliveries. Management has been explicit and public that Pratt & Whitney GTF engine shortages — driven by RTX prioritizing engines for in-service fleet support/MRO over new production — are the binding constraint on the A320 Family ramp, and has indicated it is pressing Pratt & Whitney under the terms of its supply contract. FY2026 guidance is stated 'before M&A' and assumes no further disruption to global trade, air traffic, the supply chain, or Airbus's own operations, and explicitly includes currently applicable tariffs.

bull_case: Effective duopoly with Boeing in large commercial aircraft, with Airbus currently outperforming on both deliveries and order intake while Boeing works through 737 MAX/787 quality and production recovery
Record order backlog (9,222 aircraft at H1 2026, ~8-9 years of current production) provides exceptional multi-year revenue visibility largely insulated from near-term demand shocks
Multiple simultaneous production rate ramps (A220, A320 Family, A330, A350) each represent a multi-year runway of volume-driven revenue and margin growth once engine supply constraints ease

European/NATO defense spending increases are driving record order intake and margin improvement in the previously underperforming Defence and Space segment, diversifying growth beyond commercial cyclicality

Spirit AeroSystems structures acquisition improves supply chain security and long-term cost control over critical A220/A320/A350 work packages, reducing single-supplier risk that has plagued the industry
bear_case: Pratt & Whitney GTF engine shortages have already forced Airbus to repeatedly push back A320 Family rate targets, showing limited control over its own critical supply chain even with a record backlog

Defence and Space has a history of large impairments and cost overruns (OneSat satellites, A400M legacy losses); the segment's margin recovery is not yet fully proven and announced job cuts carry execution risk
Spirit AeroSystems integration brought an immediate EUR749m FY2025 charge and ongoing purchase price allocation uncertainty through end-2026, with full cost-absorption risk still unresolved

Negative free cash flow before customer financing in H1 2026 (-EUR1,166m) illustrates how working-capital-intensive the ramp-up is; FY2026 FCF guidance of ~EUR4.5bn requires a large H2 swing that has not yet been delivered
Long-term, EUR-denominated cost base against largely USD-priced aircraft creates persistent FX/hedging complexity, and tariffs are now an explicit, acknowledged drag embedded in guidance

COMAC's C919, while currently a minor and uncertified threat outside China, represents a slow-building long-term risk to the Airbus/Boeing duopoly's most profitable (narrowbody) segment, particularly in China, one of the largest growth markets
